text: Waves are the sea's sculptors. Every breaking wave slams water, air and loose stones against the shore. Over years and centuries, this wears away rock, carving cliffs, caves, arches and pillars standing alone in the water.

How fast it happens depends on the rock. Soft clay or chalk can lose a metre or more in one stormy year. Hard [[granite|granite]] might barely change in a human lifetime. That's why many coastlines zigzag, with tough rock jutting out as headlands and softer rock scooped into bays.
The sea builds as well as destroys. The sand and pebbles it grinds from cliffs get carried along the shore and dropped somewhere else, building [[@beaches|beaches]], spits and sandbars.

st.prompt: Waves carve a cave through a headland until it becomes an arch. What happens when the top of the arch falls in?

options.t: A tall pillar of rock is left standing in the sea, called a stack
The rock floats away

st.reveal: When the arch roof collapses, the seaward end is left as a lonely tower called a stack. Waves keep working on its base until it topples too, leaving a low stump that may only show at low tide.

d.try: Build a little cliff from damp sand in a tray, with a pebble wall at one end. Push water at it in gentle waves with a ruler or your hand. Watch where the sand is undercut, what happens to the overhang, and how the pebble part holds out longer.
myth: Cliffs wear away slowly and steadily, a tiny bit every day.
Waves do work at cliffs all the time, but most of the change comes in sudden falls, often during storms. A cliff can look the same for years and then lose several metres in a single night.

sec.t:
[[@waves-how|Waves]] get their energy from wind blowing over the open ocean, sometimes thousands of kilometres away. When they reach shallow water near the coast, they slow down, grow taller and crash.

When a wave hits a cliff, it squeezes air into every crack. As the wave pulls back, the air bursts out again. Over thousands of waves, this widens the cracks and loosens blocks of rock. Geographers call it hydraulic action.

Waves also throw sand, gravel and boulders at the cliff, scraping it like sandpaper. That's abrasion. Some [[@rocks-types|rocks]], such as chalk and limestone, slowly [[dissolve|dissolve]] in seawater as well.

Along the coast of Victoria in southern Australia stand the Twelve Apostles, a row of limestone stacks rising out of the Southern Ocean. Fewer than a dozen remain, and one of them crumbled in 2005.

Nearby stood London Bridge, a double arch joined to the mainland. In January 1990, the arch closest to the shore suddenly collapsed. Two visitors who had walked out to the far end found themselves cut off on a new island. Nobody was hurt, and a helicopter lifted them off.

Something similar can happen to houses. In Pacifica, California, storms in the winter of 2015–16 ate away a cliff so fast that apartment buildings at its edge had to be emptied and later pulled down.

India has more than 11,000 km of coastline, counting its islands, by a 2024 measurement, and much of it is sandy rather than rocky. At Varkala in [[@kerala|Kerala]], though, red and orange cliffs rise straight above the beach. Cliffs like these are unusual on Kerala's low, sandy coast, and they have been declared a national geological monument.

A government study of India's coast from 1990 to 2018 found that about a third of it was wearing away. Some places, such as parts of the Odisha and West Bengal coasts, have lost villages to the sea. Sea walls and rock barriers can slow the damage, though they sometimes push the problem further along the shore.

As [[@sea-level-rise|sea levels rise]] and strong storms hit more often, waves will reach higher up cliffs and beaches. Coastal towns around the world are deciding whether to build walls, plant mangroves or move back from the edge.

text: [[geologist|Geologists]] sort rocks into three big families by how they were made. Igneous rocks form when hot, molten rock cools and hardens. Sedimentary rocks form when [[@sand-where|sand]], mud, shells and other bits settle in layers and slowly turn to stone. Metamorphic rocks are older rocks that have been changed by heat and pressure deep underground, without melting.

Rocks don't stay in one family forever. Over millions of years, any rock can be worn down, buried, squeezed or melted and turned into another kind. Geologists call this slow [[@recycling|recycling]] the rock cycle.

st.prompt: The white marble of the Taj Mahal started out as a different kind of rock. Which one?

options.t: Limestone, made from shells and mud on a sea floor
Lava from a volcano
Sand blown by the wind

st.reveal: Marble is limestone that has been squeezed and heated deep underground until its grains grew into new, interlocking crystals. The rock didn't melt. It changed while still solid, which makes marble a metamorphic rock.

Wrap the layer in foil, press hard under a heavy book, then hold it in your warm hands for a few minutes. The crumbs stick into a solid, stripy lump, a little like a metamorphic rock.
myth: You can find fossils in any kind of rock.

Almost all fossils are found in sedimentary rocks, which form gently in layers of mud and sand. The heat of molten rock destroys remains, and the heat and squeezing that make metamorphic rock usually wipe fossils out.

sec.t:
Igneous comes from the [[@latin-roots|Latin]] word for fire. Deep underground, rock can be hot enough to melt into [[magma|magma]]. When magma cools slowly, far below the surface, its crystals have time to grow big. That gives [[granite|granite]], the speckled stone used for kitchen counters and many old buildings.

When magma bursts out of a [[@volcano|volcano]] as [[lava|lava]], it cools fast and the crystals stay tiny. That gives dark, fine-grained [[@earth-weird-giants-causeway|basalt]]. Much of the Deccan Plateau in western India is made of [[basalt|basalt]], laid down in giant eruptions about 66 million years ago. Some lava is so full of gas bubbles that it hardens into pumice, a rock light enough to float on water.

Rain, wind, ice and rivers slowly break rocks into grains. Rivers carry the grains away and drop them as [[sediment|sediment]] in lakes and seas. Layer after layer piles up, and the weight squeezes the lower layers. [[@minerals-everyday|Minerals in the water]] glue the grains together.

Sand becomes sandstone. Mud becomes shale. Shells and the skeletons of tiny sea creatures become limestone. The red sandstone of Delhi's Red Fort and the walls of the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] are sedimentary rocks.

Because sediment settles gently, it can bury animals and plants whole. That is why nearly all [[@fossils-form|fossils]] are found in sedimentary rock. Only a thin skin of Earth is made of these rocks, yet they cover about three quarters of the land surface.

Much of southern India sits on some of the [[@rocks-oldest|oldest rock on Earth]]. The Lalbagh Rock in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] is a mound of gneiss about 3,000 million years old. The Geological Survey of India has declared it a National Geological Monument.

The oldest known rocks, in northern Canada, are about 4 billion years old. Older rocks have been recycled away. Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old, so the rock cycle has been turning for a very long time.

A grain of sand on a beach in Goa might once have been part of a granite mountain. In millions of years, it could be buried and turned into sandstone, squeezed into a metamorphic rock called quartzite, or carried down into Earth to melt.

[[@mountains-types|Mountains rise]] as continents push together, and rain and rivers wear them down again. The Himalaya is still rising, while its rocks are already crumbling into the sand that will become new rock. Some of that crumbled rock ends up in fields as [[@soil-made|soil]].

text: Before any person went to space, scientists sent animals. Nobody knew if a living body could survive the shaking of a launch, the [[radiation|radiation]] above the air, or floating without weight. Animals went first to find out.

The earliest were fruit flies, in 1947. Then came monkeys, mice and dogs. The Soviet Union mostly sent dogs. The USA mostly sent monkeys and chimpanzees. Later flights carried cats, tortoises, frogs, fish, spiders, jellyfish, worms and tiny tough creatures called tardigrades.
Their flights showed that living things could survive space. They also raised hard questions. Some animals died, and people still debate how far it is right to use animals in research.

st.prompt: In 1973 two spiders, Anita and Arabella, went to the Skylab space station. What happened to their webs in near-weightlessness?

options.t: They managed to spin webs, though thinner and less even at first
They couldn't spin anything at all
Their silk floated away as gas

st.reveal: At first the spiders spun messy webs, but within days they built fairly good ones. Their silk was thinner in places, which suggested they were adjusting to the lack of weight.

myth: Laika was the first animal in space, and she came back safely.
Fruit flies, mice and monkeys flew before her. Laika was the first animal to orbit Earth, in 1957, but there was no plan to bring her back, and she died within hours, probably from overheating.

sec.t:
On 20 February 1947, American scientists put fruit flies on a captured German V-2 rocket at White Sands, New Mexico. The rocket climbed above 100 km, the usual border of space, and the flies parachuted back down alive.

In 1949, a rhesus monkey named Albert II reached space on another V-2. He survived the flight but died when his parachute failed. Over the next years, mice and more monkeys flew. Each flight taught engineers how to protect passengers better.

The Soviet space programme chose small, tough stray dogs from the streets of Moscow, because they were used to cold and hunger. Females were often preferred, partly because the gear for collecting their waste was simpler to design.

On 3 November 1957, a month after [[@sputnik|Sputnik]], a dog named Laika rode Sputnik 2 into [[orbit|orbit]]. She was the first animal to circle Earth. There was no way to bring her back, and she died within hours as the capsule overheated. The full story was only made public decades later.

In August 1960, two dogs, Belka and Strelka, orbited Earth for a day and landed safely. Strelka later had puppies, and one of them, Pushinka, was given to the daughter of US President John F. Kennedy.

{{story:space-body}}

On 31 January 1961, a chimpanzee named Ham flew in an American Mercury capsule. He had been trained to pull [[lever|levers]] when lights flashed, and he did so in space, proving that a pilot could work up there. Ham splashed down in the Atlantic and was picked up safely. He lived for many more years, at zoos in Washington, D.C., and North Carolina. Three months later, Yuri Gagarin became the [[@first-in-space|first human in space]].

In 1963 France sent a cat named Félicette on a short rocket flight. She came back alive.

In September 1968, the Soviet spacecraft Zond 5 carried two Russian tortoises, along with worms, flies and seeds, around the Moon and back. The tortoises lost some weight but were otherwise healthy. They were the first living things to travel around the Moon, three months before the astronauts of Apollo 8.

Later flights were less about survival and more about science. In 1973, two garden [[@spiders-silk|spiders]] named Anita and Arabella spun webs aboard the US space station Skylab. Fish, newts and jellyfish have flown to study balance and growth.

In 2007, European scientists exposed tardigrades, animals smaller than a grain of salt, to open space outside a satellite. Some survived the [[vacuum|vacuum]] and radiation and even had babies afterwards.

India hasn't flown animals, but it has sent living things. In early 2025, ISRO germinated cowpea seeds in orbit on a small experiment platform. Its human spaceflight programme, [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]], plans to send a humanoid robot called Vyommitra on test flights before any astronaut goes up.

text: An airship floats for the same reason a boat floats. A boat pushes water aside, and the water pushes back up. An airship pushes air aside. Its huge bag is filled with helium, a gas much lighter than air. If the air pushed aside weighs more than the whole airship, including its gas, frame, engines and passengers, the airship rises.

This push is called [[buoyancy|buoyancy]]. One cubic metre of helium lifts only about 1 kg, so airships have to be gigantic. Engines and [[propeller|propellers]] then push them forward, and fins steer them, much like a fish in water.

st.prompt: Roughly how much weight can one cubic metre of helium lift at sea level?

options.t: About 1 kilogram
About 100 kilograms
About 10 grams

st.reveal: A cubic metre of air weighs about 1.2 kg, and the same space filled with helium weighs under 0.2 kg. The difference, about 1 kg, is the lift. That is why airships must be enormous to carry anything.

myth: Airships float because helium has no weight.
Helium does have weight, just much less than air. An airship floats because the air it pushes aside weighs more than the airship and its gas, the same idea that lets a ship float on water.

sec.t:
A blimp has no rigid frame inside. It is a giant balloon kept in shape by the pressure of the gas, like a long party balloon. Let the gas out and it collapses into a heap of fabric. Goodyear has flown blimps over the USA since 1925, and for decades they have carried TV cameras above big American football and baseball games.

A rigid airship, often called a zeppelin after the German Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, has a skeleton of light metal girders covered in fabric. Inside are separate gas bags. Rigid airships could be built far bigger. Early gas bags were made from cow intestines, called goldbeater's skin, and one big airship needed the guts of hundreds of thousands of cattle.

Inside many airships are extra bags called ballonets, filled with ordinary air. To go down, the crew pumps air in. The airship becomes heavier and sinks. To go up, they let air out. It works like a fish's swim bladder or a submarine's tanks.

Pilots also tilt the nose up or down and use engine power, a bit like an aeroplane. Landing is the hard part. A gust can push a huge, light airship sideways, so ground crews used to grab ropes and pull it down by hand.

The Hindenburg was filled with [[@hydrogen-fuel|hydrogen]], the lightest gas of all. It gives a little more lift than helium, but it burns. The USA controlled most of the world's helium at the time and would not sell it to Germany.

On 6 May 1937, as the Hindenburg came in to land at Lakehurst, New Jersey, it caught fire. In about half a minute it was gone. Thirty-six people died, though most passengers survived. Newsreel film shocked the world, and the age of the giant passenger airship ended almost overnight.

Helium cannot burn, and modern airships use it. But helium is rare and comes from natural gas wells. Once it leaks out, it floats away into space.

Airships are making a quiet comeback. In 2024, a new rigid airship called Pathfinder 1, about 122 m long, began test flights in California. In 2025, India's defence research agency DRDO tested a small airship that climbed to about 17 km, higher than airliners fly. Airships use far less fuel than planes and can hover for days, so people hope to use them for carrying cargo to remote places. A [[@weather-balloons|weather balloon]] goes even higher, about 30 km, until it swells so much in the thin air that it bursts.

text: Frogs need water for their eggs and tadpoles, so the [[monsoon|monsoon]] is their breeding season.
Each frog [[species|species]] has a different call, so females can find the right partner.
The Western Ghats are home to hundreds of frog species found nowhere else.

Most of the singers are males. Each one pumps air back and forth over his vocal cords and into a stretchy throat pouch called a vocal sac. The sac swells like a [[@bubbles-round|bubble]] and makes his call louder. On a wet monsoon night, a single pond can hold hundreds of calling males, each trying to be heard over the rest.

frames.cap: The monsoon fills ponds and streams. It's the perfect time for frogs to lay eggs.
Male frogs puff up their throats and call loudly to attract females. Each kind has its own song.
The purple frog of the Western Ghats lives underground, eating termites. It surfaces only during the monsoon to breed.
Its closest relatives live in the Seychelles, islands that broke off from India long ago!

quiz.reveal: Male dancing frogs stretch out a back leg and wave their webbed toes, a move called foot-flagging. Against the white noise of a stream, a waving foot is easier to spot than a call is to hear. They still call too.

d.try: Make a frog's vocal sac. Blow gently into a balloon until it is half full and hold the neck shut. Hum a low note with your lips against the balloon's neck, then let a little air out as you hum. Feel the balloon buzz. A frog's stretchy throat pouch works a bit like this, making its call louder.
myth: Frogs fall from the sky with the rain, which is why they suddenly appear after a monsoon storm.

The frogs were there all along, hiding underground, under stones or in cracks during the dry months. Rain softens the soil and fills the ponds, and they come out all at once. Strong winds have very rarely carried small animals into the sky, but that is not what happens in an ordinary monsoon.

sec.t:
For much of the year, India is too dry for frog eggs. Frog eggs have no shell, and tadpoles must live in water, so a frog that breeds in the dry season would lose its young. So many frogs spend the hot months hidden, buried in soil, tucked under rocks or curled inside cracks, using very little energy.

When the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] arrives, ponds, ditches and paddy fields fill almost overnight. Frogs pour out to mate and lay eggs while the water lasts. The whole frog year is timed to the rains.

Beside fast, noisy streams in the Western Ghats live the dancing frogs. Over the roar of the water, a call is hard to hear. So the males stretch out a back leg and wave their webbed toes at females, a move called foot-flagging. In 2014, Indian scientists led by S.D. Biju described 14 new species of these frogs at once.

In the plains, the big Indian bullfrog has its own monsoon costume. For a few days of breeding, the males turn bright lemon yellow, with two balloon-like blue vocal sacs puffing out at their cheeks.

Frogs everywhere sing to find partners. In the eastern USA, tiny frogs called spring peepers start singing in ponds as winter ends, so loud that a marsh sounds like jingling bells. [[@birds-sing|Birds]] have dawn choruses too, but frog choruses usually come at night.

In some parts of India, people have long held mock "frog weddings" in dry years, hoping to bring rain. The custom shows how closely frogs and rain are linked in people's minds.

Frogs are in trouble around the world. Over the past few decades, a disease caused by a chytrid [[fungus|fungus]] has wiped out or badly harmed hundreds of frog species, especially in Central America and Australia. Frogs also lose their homes when [[@wetlands|wetlands]] are drained and streams are polluted.

Frogs breathe partly through their thin, damp [[@skin|skin]], so poisons in water reach them easily. When frogs disappear from a place, it is often an early warning that something has gone wrong with its water. A noisy pond on a monsoon night is a sign of a healthy one.

text: When plants or animals arrive somewhere new, most don't survive, or settle in quietly. But a few take over. These are called invasive [[species|species]]. Away from the [[predator|predators]], diseases and competitors that kept them in check at home, they can multiply fast. They may eat local animals, crowd out local plants or spread disease.

People have moved species around for thousands of years, sometimes on purpose, as crops, pets or garden plants, and sometimes by accident, in ships and cargo. A 2023 global report estimated that invasive species cost the world more than 423 billion US dollars in the year 2019, through damage to crops, forests, fisheries and health.

sec.t:
In 1935, Australian sugarcane growers had a problem with beetles. Someone suggested cane toads, large toads from Central and South America. About a hundred were shipped to Queensland from Hawaii, where they had already been introduced. They were bred, and a few thousand young toads were released into the cane fields.

The toads ignored most of the beetles. Instead, they ate almost anything else they could fit in their mouths and bred quickly, laying thousands of eggs at a time. Worse, their skin [[gland|glands]] hold a strong poison. Native Australian snakes, lizards and small hunting [[marsupial|marsupials]] called quolls had never met them and died after eating them. Today the toads have spread across a large part of northern and eastern [[@australia|Australia]].

India has its own invaders. Lantana, a shrub with clusters of pink, orange and yellow flowers, was brought from the Americas by the British as a garden plant in the 1800s. It escaped and now forms thick tangles in many forests, crowding out the grasses and plants that deer and elephants eat.

Water hyacinth, a floating plant from South America with lilac flowers, can cover lakes in a green carpet, blocking sunlight and boats. In Kutch, a thorny tree called vilayati babul, or Prosopis, was planted to stop deserts spreading. It has since invaded the Banni grasslands, one of the largest grasslands in Asia, where herders graze their buffaloes.

Some people are turning these weeds into something useful. In parts of southern India, craft workers bend lantana stems into chairs and baskets, and in Assam and elsewhere, dried water hyacinth is woven into mats and bags.

{{story:columbus}}

In 1890, a man named Eugene Schieffelin released about 60 [[@sky-murmurations|European starlings]] in Central Park, New York. Today tens of millions of starlings live across North America, competing with native birds for nest holes.

In the late 1980s, zebra mussels, small striped shellfish from the region around the Black and Caspian Seas, turned up in the [[@great-lakes|Great Lakes]], probably carried in water from ships. They now clog water pipes and smother native mussels. In Florida, Burmese pythons, many likely escaped or released pets, have spread through the Everglades.

Many of the world's most loved foods are introduced species. After [[@columbus|Columbus]] crossed the Atlantic in 1492, plants and animals began moving between the continents. [[@chillies|Chillies]], potatoes and tomatoes came to India from the Americas, mostly through Portuguese traders. Wheat, cows and horses went the other way to the Americas.

Scientists now try to stop new invaders before they arrive, by checking cargo, cleaning ship [[ballast|ballast]] water and asking travellers not to carry plants or animals across borders. Stopping an invader early is far easier than removing it later.

text: A smoke alarm has a small [[sensor|sensor]] that notices tiny particles of smoke in the air. When enough smoke drifts inside, the sensor triggers a loud alarm, loud enough to wake most adults in the middle of the night.

There are two main kinds. Ionisation alarms use a tiny amount of radioactive material to make the air inside a little chamber carry a weak electric current. Smoke gets in the way of that current, and the alarm goes off. Photoelectric alarms use light instead. A small light shines inside a dark chamber, and when smoke floats in, it scatters the light onto a sensor. Many alarms today combine both.

st.prompt: Why are smoke alarms usually fixed on the ceiling and not low on the wall?

options.t: Hot smoke rises, so it reaches the ceiling first
To keep them out of reach of children
Because the batteries last longer up there

st.reveal: Smoke from a fire is carried upwards by hot air. It spreads across the ceiling first, then slowly fills the room downwards, so an alarm up high gets the earliest warning.

myth: The radioactive material in smoke alarms makes them dangerous to have at home.

The amount is tiny and sealed inside a metal case. The radiation it gives off outside the alarm is far less than what you get naturally from rocks, food and the sky. The only rule is not to open or break the alarm.

sec.t:
Inside an ionisation alarm are two small metal plates, close together, with a battery connected across them. Next to them sits a speck of americium-241, a [[radioactive|radioactive]] metal. It gives off tiny particles that knock [[electron|electrons]] off the air [[molecule|molecules]] between the plates. The air becomes charged, so a weak electric current flows across the gap.

When smoke gets in, the smoke particles grab those charged bits of air. The current drops. A small [[circuit|circuit]] notices the drop and sets off the alarm. Ionisation alarms are very quick to sense fast, flaming fires, which make lots of tiny smoke particles.

The americium [[@half-life|decays]] slowly, losing half its radioactivity in about 430 years, so it lasts far longer than the alarm itself.

In the 1930s, the Swiss physicist Walter Jaeger was trying to invent a device to detect poison gas. His design used ionised air, but the gas had no effect. According to the story often told, he lit a cigarette in frustration and the meter jumped. He had found a smoke detector instead.

Home smoke alarms became cheap and common in the United States in the 1970s, once small battery-powered models were sold. In the US, about three in five home fire deaths happen in homes without working smoke alarms, according to the National Fire Protection Association.

A short chirp every minute or so usually means the battery is running low, not that there's a fire. That chirp is designed to be annoying, so someone fixes it. People sometimes take the battery out to stop beeping when they cook, then forget to put it back. Firefighters say this is one of the most common reasons alarms fail.

Alarms don't last forever. Most need replacing after about ten years, and the date is often printed on the back.

In India, offices, malls, hotels, hospitals and tall apartment blocks are required by building and fire safety rules to have smoke detection systems. In ordinary homes they are much less common than in the US or UK.

[[@kitchen-safety|Kitchens]] cause many home fires, but an alarm right next to a stove will go off every time someone fries puris. That's why experts suggest putting alarms near bedrooms and in hallways, not right above the cooker. Studies have also found that many children sleep through smoke alarms, so families should have a fire plan that includes waking them. [[@jobs-firefighter|Firefighters]] often visit schools to teach children what to do when they hear one.

text: When you flush, [[@how-water-tank-overflow|water from the tank]] rushes into the bowl. It fills the curved pipe below so fast that it starts a siphon, a strong pull that sucks the water and waste down and away. Then the bowl refills, leaving a little water at the bottom to block smells.

From there, the waste water travels through pipes under your home into bigger pipes under the street, called sewers. They slope gently downhill, so [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] does most of the work, with pumps helping where the ground is flat. The sewers lead to a treatment plant, where the water is cleaned and returned to a river or the sea. In many Indian towns and villages, homes use septic tanks instead, which hold and break down the waste underground.

The toilet hasn't finished draining

st.reveal: The pipe below the bowl bends up and then down again. Water settles in the low part and seals the pipe like a plug. Air and smells from the sewer can't get past it. After every flush, the bowl refills enough to make a new seal.

Blow gently into one end. The water moves, but air can't get through without pushing it out, just like the seal under a toilet.
myth: Thomas Crapper invented the flush toilet.

Flush toilets go back at least to 1596, when Sir John Harington built one for Queen Elizabeth I. Alexander Cumming patented the S-bend in 1775. Thomas Crapper was a London plumber in the late 1800s who improved and popularised toilets, but he didn't invent them.

sec.h: The bend that saves your nose
sec.t:
The pipe below every toilet, sink and shower has a bend in it, shaped like a U or an S. Water always settles in the low part and stays there. This small pool seals the pipe, stopping foul-smelling gases in the sewer from drifting back up into your bathroom.

The Scottish watchmaker Alexander Cumming patented this S-shaped bend in 1775. It was a simple idea, but it made indoor toilets much more pleasant. Before it, many homes in Europe used chamber pots, and many Indian homes had toilets outside, away from the living rooms. A bend full of water let the toilet move indoors.

By the 1850s, [[@london|London]] had more than two million people, and much of their waste flowed straight into the River Thames. Cholera outbreaks killed thousands. In the hot summer of 1858, the smell from the river was so bad that it became known as the Great Stink. Members of Parliament, sitting right beside the Thames, hung curtains soaked in chemicals over the windows.

That finally pushed the government to act. The engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed a network of huge brick sewers that carried waste east, away from the city centre. Much of it, built from 1859 into the 1870s, is still in use today.

At a modern treatment plant, the first step is to screen out rags, plastic and grit. Then the waste water rests in big tanks so heavier material sinks. Next comes the clever part. Air is bubbled through the water, and huge numbers of helpful [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]] feed on the waste, breaking it down. The cleaned water settles once more and may be disinfected before it flows into a river.

The leftover sludge can even be turned into [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] or into [[@biogas|biogas]], a fuel. Since 2014, India's Swachh Bharat Mission has built many millions of toilets. The UN marks World Toilet Day every 19 November, because billions of people still lack safe sanitation.

text: Lakh and crore are Indian words for big numbers. One lakh is a hundred thousand, written 1,00,000. One crore is ten million, written 1,00,00,000. So one crore is the same as 100 lakh.

They come from the way numbers are grouped. The international system groups digits in threes: thousand, million, billion. The Indian system groups the first three digits, then every two after that: thousand, lakh, crore. That's why the commas fall in different places. People across South Asia use these words every day, for prices, salaries, populations, film box-office records and government budgets.

st.prompt: How many lakhs make one crore?
st.reveal: One lakh is 1,00,000 and one crore is 1,00,00,000. Since one crore has two more zeros, it equals 100 lakh. In international terms, a lakh is a hundred thousand and a crore is ten million.

d.try: Write your town's or state's population in both styles, Indian and international, putting the commas in the right places. Then read each version aloud, once using lakh and crore and once using thousand and million. Ask a grown-up which way feels more natural to them.
myth: A crore is the same as a billion.
A crore is ten million. A billion is a hundred crore, which in the older Indian system is called an arab. Mixing these up can make a number seem a hundred times bigger or smaller than it really is.

sec.t:
Take the number 12345678. Written the international way, it's 12,345,678, read as "twelve million, three hundred forty-five thousand, six hundred seventy-eight".

Written the Indian way, it's 1,23,45,678, read as "one crore, twenty-three lakh, forty-five thousand, six hundred seventy-eight". The digits and their [[@place-value|place values]] are exactly the same. Only the grouping changes.

A few handy swaps help when switching between the two. Ten lakh is one million. One crore is ten million. A hundred crore is one billion. When an Indian newspaper says a city has "two crore people", an American paper would write "20 million".

sec.h: Lakh and crore in daily life
sec.t:
Look at any Indian newspaper and you'll see these words everywhere. India's [[@population|population]] is more than 140 crore people. In 2025–26, the central government planned to spend about ₹50 lakh crore, a number so big it combines both words. That's 50 followed by 12 zeros.

Films measure success the same way. When a [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] film earns more than ₹100 crore in cinemas, it is said to join the "100 crore club", a phrase that became popular after *Ghajini* in 2008. Property prices, cricket auctions and school fees all get quoted in lakh and crore.

Indian English has borrowed both words, and so have the dictionaries. The British in India used "lakh" so often that it appears in English texts from the 1600s, often spelled "lac".

The old Indian system keeps going. One hundred crore is an arab. One hundred arab is a kharab, and names continue beyond that. Few people use them today. Instead, Indians mostly stack the familiar words, saying "lakh crore" for a million million, or "hazaar crore" for ten billion.

The international system has its own ladder: million, billion, trillion, quadrillion. Even that has changed over time. In Britain, a "billion" once meant a million million, and only in 1974 did the British government officially switch to the American meaning of a thousand million. Number words, it turns out, are habits, and habits differ from place to place.

Many Indians switch between the systems without thinking, using lakh and crore at home and million and billion at work or in science. Banks and phones let you choose which comma style to show.

Mistakes still happen. A crore is not a billion, and mixing them up can make a sum seem a hundred times too big. A useful check is to count the zeros. One crore has seven. One billion has nine. When in doubt, write the number out in full.

text: Spin creates a sideways push in the air called the Magnus effect. Footballers use it to [[@sport-science-football-curve|bend free kicks]]. In cricket, it can make a ball drift a little in the air and dip sooner than expected.

When the ball bounces, [[friction|friction]] between the spinning ball and the pitch turns it sideways. The spin acts like a car's wheels gripping a road: as the ball lands, the spinning surface "bites" the ground and kicks off in a new direction.
Finger spinners and wrist spinners make the ball turn in different directions. Batters must read the bowler's hand, the ball in the air and the bounce, all in less than a second.

frames.cap: The bowler flicks the ball with fingers or wrist, so it spins fast as it flies.
In the air, the spin makes the air push a little to one side. The ball drifts and dips.
When it lands, the spinning ball grips the pitch and kicks off in a new direction.
Dry, dusty pitches grip more. That's why spinners love Indian pitches!

quiz.prompt: A wrist spinner bowls a "googly". What does it do?

options.t: It turns the opposite way from the bowler's normal ball
It bounces twice before reaching the batter
It goes straight with no spin at all

quiz.reveal: A leg-spinner's normal ball turns away from a right-handed batter. The googly is bowled with almost the same action, but turns the other way, into the batter. It was made famous by the English bowler Bernard Bosanquet around 1900.

d.try: Roll a rubber or tennis ball along a smooth floor towards a wall while twisting it with your fingers as you let go, first one way, then the other. Watch which way it moves after it hits the wall or bounces. Then try on a rug, which grips more, and compare.
myth: Spin only matters after the ball bounces. In the air, a spinning ball flies straight.
Spin also affects the ball in the air. Through the Magnus effect, a spinning ball can drift sideways and dip sooner than a batter expects, before it even lands.

sec.t:
Finger spinners, also called off-spinners when they bowl right-arm, twist the ball with their fingers as they let go. For a right-arm off-spinner, the ball usually turns into a right-handed batter from outside the off stump.

Wrist spinners flick the ball out of the back of the hand with a twist of the wrist. A right-arm leg-spinner's normal ball, the leg-break, turns the other way, away from a right-handed batter. Wrist spin is harder to control but can produce more turn and some sneaky variations, such as the googly, which turns the opposite way with almost the same action.

A spinning ball drags a thin layer of air around with it. On one side, the ball's surface moves with the passing air, and on the other, against it. The air leaves the ball unevenly, and the ball is pushed the other way, just like a [[@baseball-curve|baseball curveball]].

With overspin, the push is downward, so the ball dips and lands shorter than the batter expected. With sidespin, it can drift sideways. Bowlers also toss the ball up slower, giving it "flight", so it hangs in the air and tempts the batter forward.

In 1993, the Australian leg-spinner Shane Warne bowled his first ball in an Ashes Test in England. It drifted, pitched outside Mike Gatting's leg stump and spun back to hit the off stump. It is often called the "Ball of the Century".

In 1999, at Delhi's Feroz Shah Kotla ground, India's Anil Kumble took all ten Pakistan wickets in one innings. Only two other bowlers have done this in [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]]. Jim Laker of England did it in 1956. Ajaz Patel of New Zealand, who was born in Mumbai, did it in 2021, against India in Mumbai.

Spin science turns up in many sports. [[@tennis|Tennis]] players use topspin to make shots dip into the court. Footballers bend free kicks around walls of defenders. [[@table-tennis|Table tennis]] players add so much spin that a ball can jump sideways off the table. And a [[@yo-yo-tops|spinning top]] or [[@bicycle-balance|bicycle wheel]] shows another side of spin: things that spin fast are hard to tip over.

text: People have loved quizzes for as long as there have been questions to ask. Radio stations in the USA ran quiz programmes in the 1930s. Television made them far bigger, because viewers could see the sweat on a contestant's face and hear the clock ticking.

In India, *Kaun Banega Crorepati* became a sensation from its first episode on 3 July 2000. It was based on a British show, *Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?*, which began in 1998. With [[@amitabh-bachchan|Amitabh Bachchan]] as host, a top prize of a crore and ordinary people in the hot seat, it turned general knowledge into a national obsession.

d.try: Run a family quiz night. Write ten questions on slips of paper, getting harder as they go, and give each player one lifeline, such as asking another person for help. Keep score, and see whether the hardest questions really are the ones people get wrong.
myth: Contestants on big quiz shows are secretly given the answers.

Some American shows in the 1950s were fixed, and the scandal led to a US law in 1960 making it a crime to rig a quiz show. Big shows today use strict rules, sealed questions and outside checkers to keep the game fair.

sec.t:
American television tried quizzes early. In 1955, *The $64,000 Question* became a hit on CBS. That sum was a fortune at the time, and families gathered around the TV to watch people climb towards it, question by question.

Within three years, things went badly wrong. It turned out that producers of some shows, especially one called *Twenty-One*, had secretly given favourite contestants the answers to keep viewers hooked. When this came out in 1958, the scandal reached the US Congress. A 1960 law made fixing a quiz show a crime, and big-money quizzes almost vanished from American screens for years.

India's link with the *Millionaire* format later went global in another way. A novel by the Indian diplomat Vikas Swarup imagined a boy from Mumbai's streets answering every question on a quiz show. It became the film *Slumdog Millionaire*, which won eight Oscars in 2009.

The KBC set was dark, with a glowing hot seat in the middle and music that rose as the questions got harder. The format made every question feel like a cliffhanger. Contestants had lifelines, such as asking the audience or phoning a friend. Viewers at home played along and shouted answers at the screen.

The host mattered too. Amitabh Bachchan spoke to contestants with warmth and gentle humour. Lines like "lock kiya jaye?" (shall we lock it?) became everyday phrases. In 2000, Harshvardhan Navathe became the first person to win one crore on the show, and the news made front pages across India.

sec.h: Stories of the people in the chair
sec.t: Over the years, KBC has become as much about contestants as questions. A schoolteacher, a farmer's son or a railway clerk can tell their story to the whole country. Many winners have used their prize to build a house, pay for studies or help their village. By 2025, the top prize had grown to ₹7 crore.

Quiz shows test more than [[@memory|memory]]. Contestants must judge how sure they really are. Using a lifeline too early wastes it, while guessing at the wrong moment can cost a fortune. That is a lesson in [[@probability|probability]]: with four options and no clue, you have only a one-in-four chance of being right.

In America, *Jeopardy!* has run since 1964. In 2004, a software engineer named Ken Jennings won 74 games in a row on the show, a record that still stood in 2025. He later became its host, proof that the person who knows the most answers can end up asking the questions.

text: Most of the cities of 2050 already exist, so they will look partly like today's. But they will be bigger, hotter and, if planners succeed, greener. The UN's 2025 report found that about 45% of the world's 8.2 billion people live in cities, and that roughly two-thirds of population growth until 2050 will happen in them.

Many cities will add more [[@metro-trains|metro]] lines, electric buses, trees and shade, and use computers to run traffic, water and power. Some may try out [[@self-driving|self-driving]] taxis, farms inside buildings and roads that soak up rain. But the hardest problems are older ones: heat, floods, water, housing and traffic. How well cities handle those will matter more than any gadget.

st.reveal: The UN's 2025 report put Jakarta first with about 42 million people, followed by Dhaka in Bangladesh and then Tokyo. The ranking changed partly because the UN started measuring city areas in a new, more consistent way.

Flying taxis are being tested, but they are noisy, costly and carry few people. Most experts expect metros, buses, bicycles and walking to move far more city people in 2050, because they move crowds using little space and energy.

sec.t:
In 2025, the UN counted 33 megacities, cities of more than 10 million people. Jakarta came top with about 42 million in its urban area, followed by Dhaka and Tokyo. Several Indian cities, including Delhi, are on the list. A megacity of that size has more people than many countries.

The fastest growth is expected in Asia and Africa. Places that are towns today may be big cities by 2050. That means millions of new homes, schools, pipes and bus routes, many of which haven't been built yet.

Concrete and roads soak up heat by day and release it at night. This makes cities several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. [[climate|Climate]] change adds even more heat, and [[@heatwaves|heatwaves]] are expected to get worse.

Cities are trying fixes. In 2013, Ahmedabad created one of South Asia's first heat action plans, with early warnings and cooler public spaces. Cities from Ahmedabad to Los Angeles paint some roofs or roads white or light grey to reflect sunlight. Planting trees helps too. Shade from a single big tree can make the pavement below much cooler to stand on.

In 2015, India launched its Smart Cities Mission for 100 cities, with control rooms watching traffic cameras, water supply and streetlights. [[sensor|Sensors]] can spot leaking pipes or full rubbish bins. Apps can tell you exactly when the next bus will come. Yet the hardest part of becoming a [[@smart-cities|smart city]] is often plain good roads and drains.

Self-driving taxis already carry passengers in a few US cities, like San Francisco and Phoenix. Some people think they will be common by 2050. Others think buses and trains will matter far more, because they move many people in little space.

Some planners want cities where you can reach school, shops, a doctor and a park within 15 minutes on foot or by bicycle. Paris has made this a goal. It means mixing homes, offices and shops instead of keeping them far apart.

Tall towers made of strong engineered wood are going up in Norway and the USA, because wood stores carbon instead of releasing it. And the strangest part? Some of the ideas that feel futuristic are very old: the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] had planned streets and covered drains about 4,500 years ago.

text: A social media app is a giant website where people post photos, videos and messages, and see what others have posted. Behind the screen, a set of rules run by a computer, called an [[@algorithms|algorithm]], decides which posts to show each person and in what order.

The [[algorithm|algorithm]] watches what you tap, like, share and linger on. It then guesses what will keep you watching and shows you more of that. Most apps are free because companies earn money from adverts that appear between posts. The more time people spend, the more adverts they see.

By charging phone companies for every post

st.reveal: Advertisers pay to show their adverts to the people most likely to be interested. The longer you scroll, the more adverts you see, so apps are designed to keep your attention.

myth: If an app is free, you are not paying anything for it.
You pay with your time and attention, and often with information about what you like, where you are and who your friends are. That information helps the company sell adverts.

sec.t:
One of the first social networks, SixDegrees, appeared in 1997. It let people list their friends and see friends of friends. Facebook started in 2004 for students at Harvard University, then opened to everyone. YouTube followed in 2005, Twitter in 2006 and Instagram in 2010.

At first, most apps showed posts in the order they were made, newest first. Over time, companies switched to ranked feeds, where the algorithm picks what goes at the top. Facebook added its "Like" button in 2009, giving the algorithm a simple signal of what people enjoyed.

Many features are designed to hold attention. Infinite scroll means the feed never ends. Autoplay starts the next video before you decide. Notifications buzz to pull you back. Small rewards, like a new like or comment, arrive at unpredictable times.

Doctors and scientists are still studying what this means for children. In 2023 the US Surgeon General, America's top [[@public-health|public health]] doctor, warned that heavy use could harm some young people's sleep and mood. The same report noted that social media can also help people find friends and support. Researchers disagree about how big the effects are. Learning about [[@screen-time|screen time]] and sleep is a good place to start.

Most big apps say users must be at least 13. That limit comes from a 1998 American law, COPPA, which makes it hard for companies to collect personal information from younger children without a parent's permission. In India, a 2023 data protection law says companies need a parent's consent before handling the personal data of anyone under 18.

Some countries are going further. [[@australia|Australia]] has a law, in force since December 2025, to keep children under 16 off major social media platforms. Others are debating similar steps, and not everyone agrees on the right approach.

Social media is also where much of modern language is born, from hashtags to [[@emojis|emojis]]. Knowing the basics of [[@online-safety|online safety]], such as keeping accounts private and never sharing your address or school, matters whichever app you use.

text: Around 261 BCE, Ashoka's army conquered Kalinga, a kingdom roughly where [[@odisha|Odisha]] is today. The war was terrible. Ashoka himself later wrote that 1,50,000 people were carried away, 1,00,000 were killed and many more died afterwards.

Seeing this, he felt deep sorrow. He turned to the teachings of the [[@buddha|Buddha]] and decided to rule by *dhamma*, a word for right conduct: kindness, honesty and respect for all living things. Instead of conquering with swords, he said, he would win people over with good behaviour. We know this because he said so in his own words, carved on a rock.

st.reveal: Most edicts call the king Devanampiya Piyadasi. For years scholars weren't sure who that was. Then in 1915 an edict found at Maski in Karnataka used the name Ashoka, settling the question.

myth: After becoming a Buddhist, Ashoka got rid of his army.
He gave up wars of conquest, but he kept his army. One edict even warns forest peoples that the king, though sorry for the past, still has the power to punish.

sec.t:
The edicts are practical as well as moral. Ashoka says he planted shade trees and dug wells along [[@roads-built|roads]], and built rest houses for travellers. He arranged medical treatment for people and for animals, and grew healing herbs where they were missing.

He cut down on killing animals in the royal kitchen and banned some animal sacrifices. He asked people to respect parents, teachers and servants. He also asked followers of different faiths to speak well of each other's beliefs, a message that still sounds fresh today.

Ashoka sent messengers to kingdoms as far away as Greece and Egypt. Buddhist tradition says his son Mahinda carried Buddhism to [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], where it is still the main religion.

He supported Buddhist monks and built many [[stupa|stupas]], dome-shaped mounds holding relics. Buddhist stories later claimed he built 84,000 of them, a number meant to sound endless rather than to be counted. The great stupa at Sanchi in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] began in his reign. Most edicts are in Prakrit, a spoken language of the time, written in the Brahmi script. In the far northwest he used Greek and Aramaic so local people could read them.

At Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, Ashoka raised a pillar topped by four lions facing four directions. The lions stand above a wheel, the symbol of dhamma.

When India became a [[republic|republic]] in 1950, the Lion Capital became the national emblem. The wheel, called the Ashoka Chakra, sits in the middle of the [[@flags|national flag]]. A king who gave up war is now on every passport and coin.

After the Mauryas fell, people forgot how to read Brahmi. Ashoka became a hazy name in Buddhist legends. In 1837, James Prinsep, a British official at the Calcutta mint, worked out the script by comparing [[inscription|inscriptions]] and coins.

At first, the king in the edicts was a mystery called Piyadasi. Only in 1915 did a newly found edict name him as Ashoka. Historians still argue about how sincere he was. Some see a true change of heart. Others see a clever ruler using kind words to hold a vast empire together. Either way, few kings have left such a personal record.

text: The Code of Hammurabi is a set of about 282 laws written by order of Hammurabi, king of [[@babylon|Babylon]], near the end of his reign around 1750 BCE. The laws cover everyday life: buying and selling, borrowing money, renting fields, marriage, theft, injuries, wages and building houses.

The best-known copy is carved on a tall black stone slab called a [[stele|stele]], about 2.25 metres high. It is covered in wedge-shaped [[@writing-began|cuneiform]] writing in the Akkadian language. Today it stands in the Louvre Museum in Paris, where crowds walk all the way around it to see the tiny, neat signs.

st.prompt: Under Hammurabi's laws, if a builder put up a house that fell down and killed the owner, what happened to the builder?

options.t: The builder was put to death
The builder paid a small fine
Nothing, because accidents were nobody's fault

st.reveal: Law 229 says the builder shall be put to death. Many of Hammurabi's punishments were harsh by modern standards, but this law also shows something new for its time, the idea that a worker is responsible for the safety of what he builds.

myth: The Code of Hammurabi was the first written law code in history.
It is the most famous and one of the most complete, but older ones exist. The laws of Ur-Nammu, from the Sumerian city of Ur, were written about 300 years earlier.
facts: Hammurabi of Babylon, ruled about 1792–1750 BCE
a black basalt stone about 2.25 m tall

sec.h: A king and a sun god
sec.t:
At the top of the stone is a carved picture. Hammurabi stands with one hand raised in respect before Shamash, the sun god and god of justice, who sits on a throne. The message was clear: the king's laws had the gods' approval.

Below comes a long introduction, in which Hammurabi says he was chosen "to make justice appear in the land" and to stop the strong from harming the weak. Then come the laws. At the end, he curses any future king who dares to change them. Letters Hammurabi sent to his officials also survive, giving orders about canals, taxes and court cases.

The laws did not treat all people the same. Babylonian society had three main groups: free people of high rank, ordinary free people, and enslaved people. Hurting a high-ranking person brought the harshest punishment. Hurting an ordinary person often meant paying silver. Hurting an enslaved person usually meant paying the owner.

Some laws protected women, for example by letting a wife keep her dowry if her husband left her. Others gave fathers and husbands much more power than we would accept today. Historians still argue about whether judges used the code word for word, or whether it was more like a royal list of good examples.

The stone probably once stood in a temple in the city of Sippar, and other copies were set up elsewhere. Around 1150 BCE, a king of Elam, a kingdom to the east, raided Mesopotamia and carried the stone back to his capital, Susa, in today's Iran. A few lines near the bottom were scraped away, perhaps so he could add his own words.

French [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found it at Susa in the winter of 1901 to 1902, broken into three pieces. A scholar translated it within months, and it soon became famous worldwide.

Hammurabi's laws were copied by Babylonian students for more than a thousand years. Today his face looks down from a marble panel in the US House of Representatives. He also appears, alongside other famous lawgivers, on a carved frieze inside the courtroom of the US Supreme Court. Modern [[@courts-judges|courts]] follow very different ideas, but the belief that laws should be written down for all to see, rather than kept in a ruler's head, goes back a long way. Centuries later, documents like the [[@magna-carta|Magna Carta]] built on that same idea.

text: Britain skipped 11 days in 1752 because its calendar had slowly drifted away from the seasons. For centuries it had used the Julian calendar, which counted a year as exactly 365¼ days. The real year is about 11 minutes shorter.

Eleven minutes doesn't sound much, but it adds up to about one whole day every 128 years. By 1752 the calendar was 11 days out of step with the Sun. So Parliament ordered a fix. In Britain and its colonies, including those in America and parts of India, Wednesday 2 September 1752 was followed by Thursday 14 September.

st.prompt: When Britain dropped 11 days in 1752, what happened to the days of the week?

options.t: They carried on in order, Wednesday then Thursday
Eleven weekdays were skipped as well
A new eight-day week began

st.reveal: Only the dates jumped. The weekdays carried straight on, so Wednesday 2 September was followed by Thursday 14 September. Nobody lost a working day or a weekend.

Historians have found little or no evidence of such riots. The idea comes mostly from a 1755 painting by William Hogarth, which shows that slogan on a banner during an election. Many people grumbled, but the change went off quietly.

sec.t:
The Julian calendar was set up by the Roman leader Julius Caesar in 45 BCE. It had 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year. That made the average year 365.25 days long.

Earth actually takes about 365.2422 days to go round the Sun and bring the seasons back. The Julian year was a little too long, so dates crept later and later compared with the seasons. The spring [[equinox|equinox]], when day and night are about equal, was slowly sliding earlier in the calendar. That mattered to churches, because the date of Easter depends on it.

Britain, a Protestant country, was in no hurry to follow the Pope. For 170 years, crossing from France to England meant travelling back in time by about ten days. By 1752, after an extra Julian leap day in 1700, the gap had grown to 11 days.

[[parliament|Parliament]] finally passed the Calendar Act. As well as skipping 11 days, it moved New Year's Day. Until then, the year in England officially began on 25 March. From then on, it began on 1 January.

The change caused small puzzles. George Washington was born on 11 February 1731 by the old calendar. Under the new one, his birthday became 22 February 1732, the date Americans use today. The year changed too, because his birth had fallen before 25 March.

Officials collecting rent and [[@taxes|taxes]] didn't want to lose 11 days of money. So the tax year, which had begun on 25 March, was pushed forward to 5 April. Later, another small adjustment moved it to 6 April. In the UK, the tax year still begins on that date.

Other countries switched at different times. Russia kept the old calendar until 1918. That is why its October Revolution of 1917 is remembered in November by today's calendar. Greece changed in 1923.

Even now, the Julian calendar survives in some churches. Orthodox Christians in Russia and Serbia celebrate Christmas on 7 January, which is 25 December by the old calendar.

India has used many calendars for thousands of years, based on the Moon, the Sun or both. Festivals like Diwali and Eid move around the Gregorian calendar because they follow the Moon. In 1957 India adopted an official national calendar, the Saka calendar, alongside the Gregorian one. How so many calendars work side by side is explained in [[@indian-calendars|India's calendars]], and why the year has seasons at all comes down to the [[@seasons-why|tilt of the Earth]].

text: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 near the village of Palashi, about 150 km north of Kolkata. On one side was Siraj ud-Daulah, the young Nawab of Bengal. On the other was the British East India Company, led by Robert Clive.

The Company won, and Siraj was killed soon after. The battle was short and not very bloody. But it put a ruler chosen by the Company on Bengal's throne. Within a few years, the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] was collecting Bengal's taxes, and it went on to take control of much of India.

st.prompt: The Company's army at Plassey was much smaller. What mattered most in its win?

options.t: A secret deal with the Nawab's commander, whose troops stayed out of the fight
Far better weapons that the Nawab had never seen
A surprise attack in the middle of the night

st.reveal: Before the battle, Clive had agreed to make Mir Jafar the new Nawab if he held back. On the day, Mir Jafar's large force stood still. A sudden rainstorm that soaked the Nawab's gunpowder made things worse for Siraj ud-Daulah.

sec.t:
In the 1700s, Bengal was one of the richest places on Earth. Its farmers grew rice, sugar and indigo, and its weavers made fine cotton and silk cloth sold across Asia and Europe. Bengal's [[@textiles-india|textiles]] were so popular that European countries sometimes tried to ban them to protect their own weavers.

The Nawab of Bengal was in theory a governor under the Mughal emperor, but by then he ruled almost independently from his capital, Murshidabad. British, French and Dutch companies all had trading posts in Bengal, and each wanted special rights to trade without paying taxes.

sec.h: A young Nawab and an angry company

sec.t:
Clive made a secret deal: if Mir Jafar's troops held back, the Company would make him Nawab. On the morning of 23 June, Clive's army of about 3,000 men, most of them Indian soldiers called [[sepoy|sepoys]], lined up in a mango grove. Siraj's army was many times bigger.

The Nawab's guns opened fire, and for hours the two sides traded shots. Around midday, heavy [[@monsoon|monsoon]] rain swept over the field. The Company's men covered their gunpowder. Much of the Nawab's powder got soaked. One of Siraj's loyal commanders, Mir Madan, was killed, and Siraj was persuaded to pull back.

Mir Jafar's large force never attacked. By the afternoon, the Nawab's army was breaking up, and Siraj fled. Days later he was captured and killed.

Mir Jafar became Nawab, but the real power lay with the Company. He paid huge sums to Clive and other Company officers. When later Nawabs resisted, the Company fought again, winning the Battle of Buxar in 1764. In 1765, the Mughal emperor gave the Company the right to collect taxes in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

From that base, the Company built armies, fought the [[@mughals|Mughals]], Marathas and Mysore, and grew into a ruling power. Its rule lasted until the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]], after which the British Crown took over directly.

Today Palashi is a quiet place in West Bengal's Nadia district, with a small memorial. Many Indians see Siraj ud-Daulah as a ruler who stood up to foreign power and was betrayed, and in Bengali the name Mir Jafar has come to mean a traitor. British accounts once told Plassey as a great military victory. Most historians now agree it was won more by deals and money than by fighting.

text: Bali is a [[tropical|tropical]] island in Indonesia, the world's largest island country, just east of Java. It is small, about one and a half times the size of Goa, but packs in volcanoes, rice terraces, beaches and thousands of temples. Millions of tourists visit each year.

What makes Bali different from the rest of Indonesia is its religion. Most Indonesians are Muslim, but most Balinese follow their own form of Hinduism. It came from India more than a thousand years ago and blended with local beliefs about spirits, ancestors and nature. Many visitors from India are surprised to hear stories from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] on the island, though in very Balinese forms.

st.prompt: On Nyepi, Bali's Day of Silence, what are people expected to do?

options.t: Stay at home, with no lights, no work and no travel
Fly kites from every rooftop
Bang pots and pans all day

st.reveal: Nyepi is the Balinese New Year. For 24 hours, streets are empty, shops and the airport close, and lights stay off at night. Many people fast and meditate. The night before, though, is noisy, with parades of giant monster figures.

Use small rolls of clay or play dough to build little walls along each step, then pour a cup of water gently at the top. sec.t:
Each morning, Balinese women place small square trays of woven palm leaf on doorsteps, shrines and even car dashboards. These offerings, called canang sari, hold flower petals, a little rice and perhaps an incense stick. They are gifts to gods and spirits, made fresh every day.

Most family compounds have their own temple, and every village has several. That is why Bali is sometimes called the Island of the Gods. Temple festivals happen so often that on many days, somewhere on the island, people in white and gold clothes are carrying tall towers of fruit on their heads.

Balinese dance is precise and dramatic, with flashing eyes and fingers bent back. In the Kecak dance, a circle of men chant "chak-a-chak" while dancers act out scenes from the Ramayana. Music comes from the gamelan, an orchestra of bronze gongs and metal xylophones that shimmer when played together.

At night, in wayang kulit, a single storyteller works flat leather [[@puppetry|puppets]] behind a cloth screen lit by an oil lamp, voicing all the characters and leading the musicians.

Nyepi, the Balinese New Year, usually falls in March. The night before, villages parade ogoh-ogoh, giant monster figures made of bamboo and paper, through the streets with drums and torches, then often burn them. The next morning, everything stops. No work, no travel, no lights, no noise. Even the airport closes for a day, and tourists are asked to stay in their hotels.

In the 1850s, the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace noticed something odd. On Bali, the birds and animals were mostly like those of Asia. On Lombok, just across a narrow strait, many were like Australia's, with cockatoos and honeyeaters.

The channel between them is deep. Even in ice ages, when sea levels fell, it never dried up, so animals could not walk across. Scientists still call the boundary the Wallace Line. Bali also sits on a chain of [[@volcano|volcanoes]]: Mount Agung erupted in 1963 and again in 2017, closing the airport.

text: Greece has thousands of islands and islets scattered across the Aegean and Ionian Seas, about 200 of them home to people. There are so many because the land here is broken, stretched and partly drowned.

Millions of years ago, the movement of Earth's [[plate|plates]] crumpled this region into mountains and then pulled parts of it apart. Some land sank. When sea levels rose at the end of the last Ice Age, the sea flooded the valleys, and only the mountaintops were left showing. On top of that, volcanoes built a few islands of their own. The result is a sea full of rocky peaks, an [[archipelago|archipelago]] that has shaped Greek life for thousands of years.

Waves that slowly wore the island into a ring
An ancient harbour dug by people

st.reveal: Around 3,600 years ago, a huge eruption emptied the chamber of molten rock under the island. The ground above caved in, and the sea rushed in to fill the hole, leaving a ring of cliffs.

myth: Atlantis was a real place that historians have found.

Atlantis first appears in the writings of the philosopher Plato, around 360 BCE, probably as a story to make a point. Some people link it to Santorini's eruption, but there is no proof that Atlantis ever existed.

sec.t:
The Aegean Sea sits where the African plate pushes slowly north under the plate that carries Greece and Turkey. This squeezing and stretching cracked the land into blocks. Some rose as mountains, and others sank as basins.

During the last [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]], so much water was locked up in ice sheets that the sea was about 120 m lower than today. Many of today's islands were then hills on dry land. As the ice melted, the sea crept in, and those hills became islands. Divers have found ancient shorelines far below the waves.

With so many islands and so little flat farmland, [[@ancient-olympia|ancient Greeks]] took to the sea. They fished, traded olive oil and wine, and founded towns all around the Mediterranean. Sailing between islands, you were rarely out of sight of land.

The island of Crete, the largest, was home to the Minoans, one of Europe's earliest [[civilisation|civilisations]], with a great palace at Knossos. Greek stories are full of the sea, from Odysseus's ten-year voyage home to Poseidon, god of the waves. You can meet them in [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]]. The sea also linked the Greek city-states of [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], even while they quarrelled.

Ferries are to Greek islanders what buses and [[@india-wonder-mumbai-local|local trains]] are to people in Mumbai or New York. Children on small islands may take a boat to secondary school. In summer, tourists arrive in huge numbers, and some tiny islands see their population grow many times over.

Islands are grouped into chains. The Cyclades circle the holy island of Delos, said to be the birthplace of the god Apollo. The Dodecanese lie near Turkey, and the green Ionian Islands sit on the western side, facing Italy.

Island life has always been shaped by the weather. Strong summer winds called the meltemi blow from the north, cooling the islands and making ferry trips bumpy. Many islands are dry and get little rain, so some depend on rainwater tanks, desalination plants or water brought by boat.

Marble from the islands of Paros and Naxos was prized in ancient times. Some of the most famous Greek statues were carved from it, and quarries there still cut stone today.

text: The Panama Canal cuts across Panama, a narrow country in Central America, to link the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Before it opened in 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go all the way around the tip of South America. The canal cut about 13,000 km off that journey.

Panama is hilly, so the canal doesn't run at sea level. Instead it works like a staircase made of water. Ships enter giant boxes called locks. Gates close behind them, and water flows in from a lake high above, lifting the ship step by step, about 26 m in all. They cross the lake, then step back down to the other ocean. A full trip usually takes about 8 to 10 hours.

st.prompt: How do the old locks of the Panama Canal raise a ship up to the lake level?

options.t: Water flows down from the lake into the lock by gravity
Huge pumps push seawater into the lock
Cranes lift the ship on a platform

st.reveal: Gatun Lake sits higher than the locks, so opening valves lets lake water rush down through tunnels into the chamber. As it fills, the ship floats up. To lower a ship, water is let out towards the sea. No pumps are needed.

The old locks use fresh water from Gatun Lake and Alajuela Lake, which flows down by gravity. Each ship that passes lets millions of litres run out to sea, which is why droughts can force the canal to limit traffic.

sec.t:
At each end of the canal there is a flight of locks. Each lock is a concrete chamber with huge steel gates at both ends. The original chambers are 305 m long, about as long as three football fields.

To raise a ship, workers open valves that let water from Gatun Lake pour through tunnels in the walls into the chamber. As the water rises, the ship floats up with it, a bit like a person in a rising [[@elevators|lift]]. When it matches the next step, the gates open and the ship moves forward. To go down, the water is let out.

In the old locks, small electric railway engines called mules run along the walls. Ropes from the mules keep each ship centred, because some ships fit with only about half a metre to spare on each side.

sec.h: A lake made by a dam
sec.t:
The middle of the canal is Gatun Lake. It was created by building a [[@dams-power|dam]] across the Chagres River. When it filled, it was the biggest artificial lake in the world.

Rain feeds the lake. Every ship that passes through the old locks uses about 200 million litres of fresh water, which ends up in the sea. In 2023 and 2024, a severe [[drought|drought]] lowered the lake, and the canal had to cut the number and size of ships it allowed. In the 2024 financial year it handled about 11,200 transits. After the rains returned, it handled about 13,400 in 2025.

The USA ran the canal until 31 December 1999, when it passed to Panama. In 2016, Panama opened a second set of larger locks for the biggest modern ships. These newer locks save water by storing some of it in side basins and reusing it.

Tolls can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars for a large ship. The cheapest toll ever paid was 36 cents, in 1928, by the American writer Richard Halliburton, who swam the canal over several days. Officials weighed him and charged him as a ship. The [[@suez-canal|Suez Canal]] in Egypt is longer, but it has no locks at all, because the land there is flat.

text: Saffron is expensive because it is slow, fiddly work to make. Each thread is the [[stigma|stigma]] of a purple crocus flower, the part that catches [[pollen|pollen]]. Every flower has only three. They must be picked by hand, in the few weeks of autumn when the flowers bloom, usually early in the morning before the petals wilt.

It takes about 1.5 lakh flowers to make one kilogram of dried saffron. No machine does this job well, so it all comes down to human fingers. A kilogram can cost a few lakh rupees, or thousands of dollars. Luckily, a pinch of a dozen threads is enough to colour a whole pot of [[@biryani|biryani]].

options.t: Three
About fifty
One

st.reveal: Each flower has just three red stigmas. That is why you need around 1.5 lakh flowers, all picked by hand, to fill a one-kilogram box.

d.try: Drop two or three saffron threads into a small glass of room-temperature water and watch for 15 minutes. Real saffron slowly sends out golden-yellow streaks while the threads stay red. Compare it with a pinch of turmeric in another glass and see how differently they behave.
myth: If saffron turns water bright red straight away, it is good saffron.
Real saffron colours water slowly, and the colour is golden yellow, not red. A sudden red cloud is often a sign of threads that have been dyed, which is a common trick with fake saffron.

sec.t:
The saffron crocus, *Crocus sativus*, has a strange secret. It cannot make seeds that grow into new plants. [[botanist|Botanists]] think it was bred long ago from a wild crocus, and it lost the ability somewhere along the way.

So farmers do the job for it. Under the ground, each plant has a corm, a round, bulb-like food store. Every year it grows small new corms beside it. Farmers dig them up, split them and plant them in new rows. Every saffron field in Iran, Spain and Kashmir comes from corms passed from hand to hand for thousands of years.

People have prized saffron for at least 3,500 years. On the Greek island of Santorini, a wall painting from the Bronze Age shows young women gathering crocus flowers into baskets. It was buried by a volcanic eruption and dug up in the 20th century.

Saffron was used as a dye and a [[@oddity-old-medicine|medicine]] as well as a food. In India, the deep orange-yellow colour named after it became linked with holiness and with giving up worldly things. Its name probably comes from *zaʿfarān*, an Arabic word, and in Hindi and many Indian languages it is called kesar.

Saffron does three jobs at once. A natural [[@art-materials|pigment]] called crocin turns food golden. Another chemical gives a slightly bitter, honey-like taste. A third, called safranal, gives the smell that people describe as hay or honey.

That is why cooks use so little. Saffron goes into kesar pedas, kheer, Kashmiri kahwa tea and Lucknow biryani. In Spain it colours paella, and in Milan it turns risotto yellow. Iran grows about nine out of every ten threads in the world, and Persian cooks use it in rice dishes too.

Anything this costly gets copied. People have sold dyed corn silk, safflower petals and even shredded paper as saffron. In [[medieval|medieval]] Germany, selling fake saffron could get a trader punished severely.

Today, a few simple checks help. Real threads are trumpet-shaped at one end. They should smell of honey and hay, not of nothing. In water, they colour it slowly and keep their own red colour. Many shoppers also buy from trusted [[@spices|spice]] sellers, because a cheap price is usually the biggest clue of all.
